ch02.anchor: West of my lodging was Qu Qiubai
ch02.note: Qu Qiubai (1899–1935), a writer and literary critic who became the Party's effective leader at the August 7 Conference of 1927 and presided over the failed “putschist” risings that followed, before he was pushed aside. Captured by Nationalist troops in Fujian, he was executed by firing squad in 1935. (Corroborated.)

Su Zhaozheng (1885–1929), a Cantonese seaman who became the foremost labor leader of the early Party: chairman of the Seamen's Union, a leader of the 1922 Hong Kong seamen's strike and the great Canton–Hong Kong strike of 1925–26, and briefly a minister in the 1927 Guangzhou Soviet. He died in Shanghai in February 1929; his burial is described later in this chapter. (Corroborated.)

Liu Shaoqi (1898–1969), in these years a leading labor organizer—of the Anyuan miners' strike and the All-China Federation of Trade Unions—and later chairman, head of state, of the People's Republic from 1959. Purged as the foremost “capitalist roader” of the Cultural Revolution, he died in detention in 1969. (Corroborated.)

Xiang Ying (c. 1898–1941), a Wuhan textile worker turned senior Party organizer who rose to be deputy commander and political commissar of the New Fourth Army. After the Nationalists destroyed the army's headquarters in the New Fourth Army Incident of January 1941, he was killed in hiding by a subordinate who made off with its funds. His birth year is given variously as 1895 or 1898. (Corroborated.)

ch02.anchor: struck at He Mengxiong, Lin Yunan, Li Qiushi
ch02.note: He Mengxiong (1898–1931), a founding-generation Communist and northern labor leader who opposed the Wang Ming group and the Comintern's Pavel Mif at this Fourth Plenum. Arrested in Shanghai in January 1931, he was secretly shot at Longhua on 7 February 1931—one of the “twenty-four Longhua martyrs,” killed the same night as the “Five Martyrs” of the League of Left-Wing Writers (Rou Shi and the others). (Corroborated.)

ch02.anchor: rescued through the China Relief Society
ch02.note: The China Relief Society (中国济难会), a legal-aid and relief body the Communists organized in Shanghai in 1925 to help revolutionaries who had been killed, wounded, or jailed, and their families, without regard to party. It was the Chinese counterpart of the Comintern's International Red Aid (MOPR)—the “International Red Aid” named just below—and was reorganized in 1929 as the China Revolutionary Mutual Aid Society. (Corroborated; the tie to MOPR is stated in Chinese sources.)

ch03.anchor: the first Eastern Expedition against Chen Jiongming
ch03.note: The Eastern Expeditions of 1925, two campaigns the Kuomintang's Canton government launched against Chen Jiongming (1878–1933), the Guangdong warlord who had broken with Sun Yat-sen and shelled his headquarters in 1922. Spearheaded by Whampoa cadets under Soviet advice, they broke Chen's forces and drove him into exile in Hong Kong. (Corroborated.)

He Yingqin (1890–1987), chief instructor at the Whampoa academy and one of Chiang Kai-shek's most senior and loyal generals; later Nationalist minister of national defense and, briefly, premier. He ended his career on Taiwan. (Corroborated.)

Tang Shengzhi (1889–1970), a Hunanese general of the Northern Expedition who governed Hunan and later broke with Chiang Kai-shek. He is best remembered as the commander of the doomed defense of Nanjing in December 1937; he lived out his last years under the People's Republic. (Corroborated.)

Ye Jianying (1897–1986), a Whampoa instructor who joined the Communists in 1927 and helped lead the Guangzhou Uprising that December. Made a marshal in 1955, he was the senior figure who, after Mao's death, engineered the 1976 arrest of the Gang of Four, and later served as head of state. (Corroborated.)

ch03.anchor: the Third Division's commander, Zhou Yiqun
ch03.note: Zhou Yiqun (1896–1931), a Whampoa-trained political organizer and He Long's close partner; the two went on together to found the Honghu base in western Hunan and Hubei. He was killed in a Nationalist ambush in 1931. (Corroborated.)

ch03.anchor: the Army Military Academy that Sun Yat-sen had founded
ch03.note: Sun Yat-sen (孙中山, 1866–1925), the revolutionary who led the overthrow of the Qing dynasty in 1911, founded the Kuomintang, briefly served as the Republic's first provisional president, and framed the “Three Principles of the People.” Honored by Nationalists and Communists alike as the founder of modern China, he opened the Whampoa academy in 1924 with Soviet help. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: the May Fourth Movement and the new-culture currents
ch04.note: The May Fourth Movement (五四运动) began on 4 May 1919, when Beijing students protested the Versailles settlement's award of Germany's holdings in Shandong to Japan. It grew into a broad current of nationalism and cultural renewal—the “New Culture” movement—from which many founders of the Chinese Communist Party emerged. (Corroborated.)

The Tongmenghui (同盟会), or Revolutionary Alliance, the secret society Sun Yat-sen and others founded in Tokyo in 1905 to overthrow the Qing dynasty. It organized a string of anti-Qing risings, became the backbone of the 1911 Revolution, and was the forerunner of the Kuomintang. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: against the Qing and against Yuan Shikai
ch04.note: Yuan Shikai (1859–1916), the late-Qing general who turned the 1911 Revolution to his own account, became the new Republic's first president, and then, in 1915–16, tried to make himself emperor. Forced to give up the throne after eighty-three days amid a nationwide revolt, he died soon after. (Corroborated.)

Li Dazhao (1888–1927), co-founder of the Chinese Communist Party with Chen Duxiu and one of China's first Marxists; as head librarian of Peking University he was an early influence on the young Mao Zedong. Seized from the Soviet embassy compound in Beijing by the warlord Zhang Zuolin, he was hanged on 28 April 1927, the Party's first great martyr. (Corroborated.)

Cai Hesen (1895–1931), a founding Communist intellectual and close associate of Mao Zedong, an early champion of Bolshevism among the work-study students in France and an editor of the Party organ The Guide. Betrayed and arrested in Hong Kong, he was handed to the Canton authorities and executed in 1931. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: After the Xi'an Incident, the Chinese Communist Party Center sent Zhang Yunyi
ch04.note: The Xi'an Incident of December 1936: the “Young Marshal” Zhang Xueliang seized Chiang Kai-shek at Xi'an and held him until he agreed to stop the war on the Communists and turn against the Japanese invasion. Zhou Enlai took part in the negotiations; the result was the second Kuomintang–Communist united front. It falls just after this book's years and closed the underground era it describes. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: run by Deng Yanda and Yun Daiying
ch04.note: Deng Yanda (1895–1931), the Kuomintang left's foremost military-political figure, who broke with the Nationalist leadership and in 1930 founded the “Third Party.” Chiang Kai-shek's agents seized him in 1931 and had him secretly shot near Nanjing. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: on the recommendation of Sun Bingwen and Zhu De
ch04.note: Sun Bingwen (1885–1927), a revolutionary who went to Germany with Zhu De in 1922 and joined the Party there; here the two of them together sponsor Liu Ding. He was executed by the Kuomintang at Longhua in the 1927 purge. His daughter Sun Weishi, a pioneering theater director, was later adopted by Zhou Enlai and Deng Yingchao. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: the Kuomintang Reorganizationists under Hu Hanmin
ch04.note: The Reorganizationists (改组派) were a Kuomintang faction of 1928–31 that looked to Wang Jingwei and sought to “reorganize” the party against Chiang Kai-shek. The book's “under Hu Hanmin” is loose: Hu Hanmin (1879–1936) led a separate, right-wing opposition to Chiang, not the Reorganizationists, who took their lead from Wang Jingwei. (The faction's tie to Wang Jingwei, not Hu Hanmin, is the corroborated one.)

ch04.anchor: Peng Pai, Yang Yin, and others were arrested and murdered
ch04.note: Yang Yin (1892–1929), a leader of the Canton–Hong Kong strike and of the 1927 Guangzhou Uprising, and by 1929 head of the Party's military and security work. Arrested with Peng Pai after an informer's betrayal, he was secretly shot at Longhua on 30 August 1929. (Corroborated.)

ch05.anchor: Zhang Xun's attempt in the capital
ch05.note: In July 1917 the general Zhang Xun (1854–1923), the “Pigtail General” whose troops kept their Qing queues, marched into Beijing and briefly put the deposed boy emperor Puyi—whose reign title was Xuantong—back on the throne. The restoration collapsed in under two weeks. (Corroborated.)

Chen Diaoyuan (1886–1943), a former Beiyang warlord who declared for the Nationalists in March 1927 and was made commander of their 37th Army and governor of Anhui. The book calls him a “ticket bandit” for his troops' plunder; the nickname in fact traces to the 1923 Lincheng train hijacking, in which he dealt with the bandits who had seized foreign and Chinese hostages (the “tickets”). The figure of some twenty million yuan looted in three years is the author's. (Identity corroborated; the plunder figure uncorroborated.)

ch05.anchor: Kong Xiangxi, came to the opening
ch05.note: Kong Xiangxi (1881–1967), known in the West as H. H. Kung, the American-educated banker who served the Nationalist government as minister of finance and premier. Married to the eldest of the Soong sisters and brother-in-law to Chiang Kai-shek, he was reputed one of China's richest men—hence the tag “god of wealth.” (Corroborated.)

ch05.anchor: the French-South committee secretary Li Fuchun
ch05.note: Li Fuchun (1900–1975), an early Communist who studied in France on the work-study program and helped build the Party's European branch; after 1949 he became a vice-premier and the chief architect of the People's Republic's economic planning. (Corroborated.)
